title: Long-term care planning
summary: The single largest predictable cost in late retirement, often uninsured. Decide between self-insurance, traditional LTC insurance, or hybrid policies.
detailsHtml:
The exposure

Roughly 70% of Americans turning 65 will need some form of long-term care; about 20% will need it for 5+ years (HHS/ASPE 2022). Per the 2024 CareScout (formerly Genworth) Cost of Care Survey: median annual cost of a private nursing home room is ~$127,750; semi-private ~$116,800; assisted living ~$70,800; in-home care varies widely (~$77,000 for a home health aide). Costs vary by region by 30–50%, so the medians understate the high-cost-of-living urban exposure. Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care; Medicaid covers it only after most assets are depleted.

The three approaches

Self-insurance: Defensible if your portfolio is large enough to absorb 5+ years of care costs without depleting (perhaps $1.5M+ in liquid assets). Most cost-effective if you don't need care.

Traditional LTC insurance: Premiums in the $2,000–$5,000/year range for coverage starting in your 50s or 60s. Use-it-or-lose-it: no benefit if you don't need care. Carriers have repeatedly raised premiums on existing policyholders.

Hybrid policies (life + LTC): A life insurance policy that pays the death benefit either as life insurance or as long-term care. Premiums are higher but you get value either way. Currently the most-purchased category.
